pradeep|Chemistry|0|79|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
Two things are asked for at once, but they are the same condition. Since
ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°
a **positive ΔS°** makes the −TΔS° term grow more negative as T rises, so ΔG° **falls sharply
with increasing temperature**. So the question reduces to: which reaction has a positive ΔS°?
For a gas-phase reaction that means an **increase in the number of moles of gas**. Count them,
ignoring solids.
**(a) C(graphite) + ½O₂(g) ⟶ CO(g)** ✓
gas: ½ mole in, **1** mole out. Δn(gas) = **+½**, so ΔS° is **positive** ✓
**(b) CO(g) + ½O₂(g) ⟶ CO₂(g)**
gas: 1½ in, 1 out. Δn = **−½**, ΔS° negative ✗
**(c) Mg(s) + ½O₂(g) ⟶ MgO(s)**
gas: ½ in, **0** out. Δn = **−½**, ΔS° negative ✗
**(d) ½C(graphite) + ½O₂(g) ⟶ ½CO₂(g)**
gas: ½ in, ½ out. Δn = **0**, ΔS° ≈ zero ✗
Only (a) increases the gas count.
This has real importance in metallurgy. In an **Ellingham diagram** the line for
2C + O₂ ⟶ 2CO slopes **downwards** — uniquely among the oxidation lines — precisely because
ΔS is positive. That downward slope is why carbon becomes a better and better reducing agent
as the furnace gets hotter, and why coke can reduce iron oxide at blast-furnace temperatures.
∴ C(graphite) + ½O₂(g) ⟶ CO(g).

pradeep|Chemistry|0|87|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
Spontaneity is decided by
ΔG = ΔH − TΔS < 0
**Step 1 — what the equilibrium temperature means.** At T = Te the reaction is at equilibrium,
so ΔG = 0:
0 = ΔH − Te ΔS
**Te = ΔH / ΔS**
**Step 2 — impose the signs.** Both ΔH and ΔS are **positive**, so Te is positive and the two
terms in ΔG compete: ΔH pushes against the reaction, −TΔS pushes for it.
**Step 3 — find when −TΔS wins.**
ΔH − TΔS < 0
TΔS > ΔH
T > ΔH/ΔS
**T > Te** ✓
So the reaction becomes spontaneous **above** the equilibrium temperature — option (d).
The physical reading is that an endothermic reaction that creates disorder needs **heat** to
drive it, and enough of it: below Te the energy cost dominates and nothing happens, above Te
the entropy gain takes over.
The standard example is the decomposition of limestone, CaCO₃ ⟶ CaO + CO₂, with ΔH and ΔS
both positive and Te ≈ 1100 K — which is why a lime kiln has to be run hot.
Option (c), Te > T, is the same inequality written backwards and is the natural slip; option
(b), T = Te, is equilibrium itself, where nothing proceeds in either direction.
∴ T > Te.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|89|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
**Step 1 — find ΔG° from ΔH° and ΔS°.** Work in joules throughout:
ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°
= (−54 070) − (298 × 10)
= −54 070 − 2980
= **−57 050 J mol⁻¹**
**Step 2 — relate ΔG° to K.**
ΔG° = −2·303 RT log₁₀ K
**Step 3 — substitute**, using the value the question helpfully supplies,
2·303 × 8·314 × 298 = **5705**:
−57 050 = −5705 × log K
log K = 57 050 / 5705
= **10** ✓
The two slips to avoid are mixing units — ΔH° is in **kJ** and ΔS° in **J**, so one of them
must be converted, and using −54·07 with 2980 would give nonsense — and forgetting the factor
2·303 that converts the natural logarithm to base ten.
The hint '2·303 × 8·314 × 298 = 5705' is doing the work of that whole denominator, and
noticing that 57 050 is exactly ten times 5705 finishes the question in one line.
A log K of 10 means K = 10¹⁰: the reaction lies far over towards B at equilibrium, which fits
a strongly exothermic reaction with a favourable entropy change.
∴ 10.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|90|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
Use
ΔG° = −2·303 RT log₁₀ Kp
and work in **calories**, since ΔG° is given in kcal. Take R = 2 cal K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
**Step 1 — the denominator.**
2·303 × R × T = 2·303 × 2 × 300 = **1381·8 cal mol⁻¹**
**Step 2 — convert ΔG° to calories.**
46·06 kcal mol⁻¹ = **46 060 cal mol⁻¹**
**Step 3 — solve for log Kp.**
46 060 = −1381·8 × log Kp
log Kp = −46 060 / 1381·8
= **−33·33**
**Step 4 — write the constant.**
Kp = **10⁻³³·³³** ✓
The **sign** is the heart of the question. ΔG° is **positive**, meaning the reaction is
non-spontaneous under standard conditions, so K must be very **small** — far less than one.
Any positive exponent would be wrong on inspection.
The unit conversion is the other trap: using 46·06 instead of 46 060 gives log Kp = −0·033
and Kp ≈ 0·93, which is nowhere near.
A value of 10⁻³³ means the products are essentially absent at equilibrium — for every molecule
of product there are 10³³ of reactant.
∴ 10⁻³³·³³.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|91|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
At equilibrium ΔG = 0, so
ΔH = TΔS  ⇒  **T = ΔH / ΔS**
The work is in getting ΔS from the standard entropies.
**Step 1 — ΔS for the reaction.**
½X₂ + 3⁄2 Y₂ ⟶ XY₃
ΔS = S°(products) − S°(reactants)
= 50 − [½(60) + 3⁄2(40)]
= 50 − [30 + 60]
= 50 − 90
= **−40 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹**
**Step 2 — substitute**, converting ΔH to joules:
T = ΔH / ΔS
= (−30 000) / (−40)
= **750 K** ✓
The two negatives cancel, as they must — a temperature cannot be negative, and that is itself
a check that the entropy change was computed with the right sign.
Two things decide the answer. The **stoichiometric coefficients** must multiply the entropies:
using 60 + 40 instead of 30 + 60 gives ΔS = −50 and T = 600 K, which is not offered. And the
**unit conversion**: ΔH is in kJ while ΔS is in J, so −30 must become −30 000.
This is the classic reaction type — exothermic with a negative entropy change — which is
spontaneous **below** 750 K and non-spontaneous above it. Ammonia synthesis behaves exactly
this way, which is why the Haber process is a compromise on temperature.
∴ 750 K.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|95|Pradeep Chemistry.s:
The **third law** states that the entropy of a **perfect** crystal is zero at absolute zero.
The word *perfect* is doing the work: every molecule must be in one definite, identical
orientation, so there is exactly **one** possible arrangement, and S = k ln W = k ln 1 = 0.
Some substances fail this condition. Even at 0 K their molecules can sit in **more than one
orientation** in the lattice, with essentially no energy difference between them. The
crystal freezes with those orientations randomly distributed, W > 1, and so
S = k ln W > 0 — a **residual entropy** that survives to absolute zero ✓ option (b).
The standard examples:
**Carbon monoxide.** CO and OC are almost indistinguishable in size and polarity, so each
molecule can point either way. With 2 orientations per molecule, W = 2^N and the residual
entropy is R ln 2 = **5·76 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹**, close to the measured value.
**Ice.** Each water molecule can orient its two hydrogens among four neighbouring oxygens in
several ways, giving a residual entropy of about **3·4 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹**.
Why the others are wrong: (a) impurities would spoil the crystal but are not the explanation
for residual entropy in a pure substance, and (c) the practical difficulty of **reaching**
0 K is irrelevant — residual entropy is a property of the substance, found by extrapolation,
not an experimental limitation.
∴ they attain different orientations of molecules even at absolute zero.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|101|Pradeep Chemistr.s:
The efficiency of a Carnot engine is
**η = 1 − T(sink) / T(source)**
with both temperatures in **kelvin**.
For η = 1, that is 100 %, the fraction T(sink)/T(source) must be **zero**, which requires
**T(sink) = 0 K** ✓ — absolute zero.
Now the others:
**(a) sink at 0 °C** = 273 K, not zero. With a source at, say, 373 K the efficiency would be
1 − 273/373 = 27 %, nowhere near 100 % ✗
**(c) source at 273 °C** says nothing about the sink, and no finite source temperature alone
can give 100 % ✗
**(d) source at 100 °C** likewise ✗
The deeper point is that 100 % efficiency is **impossible in practice**. The third law of
thermodynamics says absolute zero cannot be reached in a finite number of steps, so a sink at
0 K cannot be built — and that is precisely the **Kelvin–Planck statement** of the second law:
no engine working in a cycle can convert heat entirely into work.
The other way to reach η = 1 would be T(source) → ∞, which is equally unattainable.
So the Carnot efficiency sets an upper limit that real engines approach but never reach; a
modern power station manages about 40 %.
∴ sink is at 0 K.

pradeep|Chemistry|0|7|Pradeep Chemistry:
Einstein's photoelectric equation is
**KE(max) = hν − hν₀ = hν − φ**
where ν is the frequency of the incident light and φ = hν₀ is the work function of the metal.
Read it as a straight line, y = mx + c:
**y** = KE of the photoelectrons
**x** = **frequency ν** of the incident light ✓
**m** = h, Planck's constant (the slope, the same for every metal)
**c** = −φ (the intercept, characteristic of the metal)
So the kinetic energy increases **linearly with the frequency** of the incident light —
option (b).
Now the others, each of which the experiment specifically rules out:
**(a) wavelength** — the dependence is on ν = c/λ, so KE varies **inversely** with wavelength,
not linearly with it. Increasing the wavelength *decreases* the energy.
**(c) velocity of incident light** — light travels at c in vacuum whatever its colour, so
this cannot vary at all.
**(d) atomic mass of the element** — the work function depends on the metal, but through its
surface binding energy, not its atomic mass, and in any case that shifts the intercept rather
than producing the linear increase described.
The **intensity** of the light is also worth mentioning: it changes the **number** of
photoelectrons, never their energy — the observation that forced the photon picture on
physics in the first place.
∴ frequency of incident light.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|10|Pradeep Chemistry:
Bohr's theory was built for a **single electron** moving round a nucleus, so it applies only
to **one-electron (hydrogen-like) species**. With two or more electrons, the electron-electron
repulsion cannot be handled and the theory fails.
Count the electrons in each:
**(a) Be³⁺** — Z = 4, charge 3+ ⇒ 4 − 3 = **1 electron** ✓ Bohr applies
**(b) Li²⁺** — Z = 3, charge 2+ ⇒ 3 − 2 = **1 electron** ✓ applies
**(d) H** — Z = 1, neutral ⇒ **1 electron** ✓ applies (the original case)
**(c) He²⁺** — Z = 2, charge 2+ ⇒ 2 − 2 = **0 electrons** ✗
Helium with both electrons removed is a **bare nucleus** — an alpha particle. There is no
electron at all, so there are no orbits, no energy levels and nothing for Bohr's theory to
describe ✓
The trap is expecting the answer to be a species with **too many** electrons, which is the
usual reason Bohr's theory fails. Here the failure is at the other extreme: too **few**.
For the three that do work, the energy levels are
Eₙ = −13·6 Z²/n² eV
so Li²⁺ and Be³⁺ have levels 9 and 16 times deeper than hydrogen's — the Z² factor being the
only change.
∴ He²⁺.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|11|Pradeep Chemistry:
For an electron bound in an atom, the kinetic, potential and total energies are locked
together by the **virial theorem**:
**KE = −E(total)**  and  **PE = 2 × E(total)**
So once the total energy is known, both others follow immediately.
The first excited state of hydrogen is n = 2, and the question gives
E(total) = **−3·4 eV**
Therefore
KE = −(−3·4) = **+3·4 eV** ✓
and, for completeness, PE = 2(−3·4) = −6·8 eV. Check: KE + PE = 3·4 − 6·8 = −3·4 ✓
The **signs** carry the physics. The potential energy is negative because the electron is
attracted to the nucleus and work must be done to pull it away; the kinetic energy is
positive, as kinetic energy always is; and the total is negative, which is precisely what
'bound' means.
The common errors are offered as distractors: **−13·6 eV** is the total energy of the
**ground** state, not the first excited state; **+13·6 eV** is its magnitude; and **+6·8 eV**
is the magnitude of the potential energy, obtained by doubling instead of negating.
A quick check on n = 2: Eₙ = −13·6/n² = −13·6/4 = −3·4 eV ✓ consistent with the data given.
∴ +3·4 eV.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|12|Pradeep Chemistry:
Energy and wavelength are inversely related:
E = hc/λ  ⇒  **the largest energy gap gives the shortest wavelength**
So find the transition with the biggest drop in energy. Using Eₙ = −13·6/n² eV:
E₁ = −13·60 eV
E₂ = −3·40 eV
E₃ = −1·51 eV
E₄ = −0·85 eV
Now the four transitions:
**(a) n₄ ⟶ n₁** : ΔE = 13·60 − 0·85 = **12·75 eV** ✓ largest
(d) n₃ ⟶ n₁ : ΔE = 13·60 − 1·51 = 12·09 eV
(b) n₂ ⟶ n₁ : ΔE = 13·60 − 3·40 = 10·20 eV
(c) n₄ ⟶ n₂ : ΔE = 3·40 − 0·85 = **2·55 eV** smallest
The largest gap belongs to n₄ ⟶ n₁, so that transition emits the **shortest wavelength** ✓
Two general rules make this quick without any arithmetic. First, transitions ending at
**n = 1** (the Lyman series) are always the most energetic, because the levels are packed
close together higher up and the n = 1 level lies far below the rest. Second, among those,
the one starting **highest** has the biggest drop.
That alone picks (a) over (d) and (b), and rules out (c), which ends at n = 2 and so belongs
to the much lower-energy Balmer series.
∴ n₄ ⟶ n₁.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|13|Pradeep Chemistry:
A fall from **infinity to n = 1** is the largest possible transition in a hydrogen atom, and
the Rydberg formula handles it directly.
**Step 1 — write the Rydberg equation.**
1/λ = R (1/n₁² − 1/n₂²)
with n₁ = 1 (the final state) and n₂ = ∞ (the initial one).
**Step 2 — substitute.** Since 1/∞² = 0,
1/λ = R (1/1 − 0) = R = **1·097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹**
**Step 3 — invert.**
λ = 1 / (1·097 × 10⁷)
= 9·11 × 10⁻⁸ m
**Step 4 — convert to nanometres**, remembering 1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m:
9·11 × 10⁻⁸ m = **91·1 nm ≈ 91 nm** ✓
The conversion at the end is where the distractors bite: option (d), 9·1 × 10⁻⁸ **nm**, is the
right figure with metres relabelled as nanometres, out by a factor of 10⁹.
This wavelength is the **series limit of the Lyman series** — the shortest wavelength hydrogen
can emit, and equivalently the **ionisation energy** of hydrogen expressed as a wavelength.
Checking that: E = hc/λ = (6·626 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3 × 10⁸)/(9·11 × 10⁻⁸) = 2·18 × 10⁻¹⁸ J, which is
**13·6 eV** ✓ exactly the ionisation energy.
At 91 nm this lies deep in the **ultraviolet**, well outside the visible range.
∴ 91 nm.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|14|Pradeep Chemistry:
Find the dimensions of h from the equation that defines it:
**E = hν**  ⇒  h = E / ν
so
[h] = energy ÷ frequency = **J ÷ s⁻¹ = J s**
Now compare that with each option:
**(a) work** — joules, J. Missing the second ✗
**(b) energy** — also joules, J ✗
**(d) linear momentum** — kg m s⁻¹. In base units J s = kg m² s⁻¹, which has an extra metre ✗
**(c) angular momentum** ✓ — angular momentum is L = mvr, with units
kg × m s⁻¹ × m = **kg m² s⁻¹ = J s** ✓ a match
The agreement is not a coincidence. Bohr's quantisation condition is exactly
mvr = **nh/2π**
so h sets the natural unit of angular momentum in quantum mechanics — which is why ħ = h/2π
is used so constantly, and why orbital angular momentum comes out as √(l(l+1)) ħ.
The quantity with dimensions of energy × time is also called **action**, and h is often
called the **quantum of action**. Its value, 6·626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, is the smallest unit in which
nature appears to transact.
∴ angular momentum.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|16|Pradeep Chemistry:
The **orbital** angular momentum of an electron is
**L = √(l(l + 1)) × ħ**  where ħ = h/2π
and l is the azimuthal quantum number, fixed by the type of orbital:
s ⟶ l = 0
p ⟶ l = 1
**d ⟶ l = 2**
f ⟶ l = 3
For a **d** orbital, l = 2:
L = √(2 × 3) ħ = **√6 ħ** ✓
The other options are the values for other orbitals, which is what makes them tempting:
√2 ħ is the p orbital (l = 1), 0 is the s orbital (l = 0), and 2√3 ħ = √12 ħ is the f orbital
(l = 3).
It is worth keeping this **orbital** angular momentum distinct from Bohr's
L = nh/2π = n ħ, which depends on the **principal** quantum number. Bohr's expression is the
older, semi-classical one and gives the wrong answer for an s electron — it predicts ħ for
the 1s electron, whereas quantum mechanics correctly gives **zero**, since l = 0.
That zero is physically meaningful: an s orbital is spherically symmetrical, with no
preferred axis for anything to circulate about.
∴ √6 ħ.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|17|Pradeep Chemistry:
**Step 1 — the energy gap between levels 1 and 2.**
E = −2·178 × 10⁻¹⁸ (Z²/n²) J, and for hydrogen Z = 1:
E₁ = −2·178 × 10⁻¹⁸ / 1 = −2·178 × 10⁻¹⁸ J
E₂ = −2·178 × 10⁻¹⁸ / 4 = −0·5445 × 10⁻¹⁸ J
ΔE = E₂ − E₁ = 2·178 × 10⁻¹⁸ (1 − ¼)
= 2·178 × 10⁻¹⁸ × 0·75
= **1·634 × 10⁻¹⁸ J**
**Step 2 — convert the energy to a wavelength.**
E = hc/λ  ⇒  λ = hc/E
hc = 6·62 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3 × 10⁸ = **1·986 × 10⁻²⁵ J m**
λ = 1·986 × 10⁻²⁵ / 1·634 × 10⁻¹⁸
= **1·216 × 10⁻⁷ m** ✓ (option b, 1·214 × 10⁻⁷ m)
The factor **¾** is the step that decides the answer: using the full 2·178 × 10⁻¹⁸ J, as if
the electron were being removed altogether, gives 9·12 × 10⁻⁸ m instead.
This wavelength, about **121·6 nm**, is the **Lyman-alpha** line — the first line of the Lyman
series, lying in the far ultraviolet. It is one of the most important lines in astronomy,
since it is how hydrogen gas between the stars announces itself.
∴ 1·214 × 10⁻⁷ m.
pradeep|Chemistry|0|19|Pradeep Chemistry:
Use the Planck relation in its wavelength form:
**E = hc / λ**
**Step 1 — convert the wavelength to metres.**
45 nm = 45 × 10⁻⁹ m = **4·5 × 10⁻⁸ m**
**Step 2 — compute hc.**
hc = 6·63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3 × 10⁸ = **1·989 × 10⁻²⁵ J m**
**Step 3 — divide.**
E = 1·989 × 10⁻²⁵ / 4·5 × 10⁻⁸
= **4·42 × 10⁻¹⁸ J** ✓
The exponent arithmetic is the whole question: 10⁻²⁵ ÷ 10⁻⁸ = 10⁻¹⁷, and 1·989/4·5 = 0·442,
so 0·442 × 10⁻¹⁷ = 4·42 × 10⁻¹⁸.
The distractors are built on the two likely errors. Options (a) and (b) are **positive** large
powers of ten, which would come from inverting the division — a single photon can never carry
10¹⁵ joules. Option (c), 4·42 × 10⁻¹⁵, is out by the nanometre conversion.
A quick order-of-magnitude check keeps you right: visible light at about 500 nm carries
roughly 4 × 10⁻¹⁹ J per photon, and 45 nm is ten times shorter, so the energy should be about
ten times larger — around 4 × 10⁻¹⁸ J ✓
At 45 nm this is extreme ultraviolet, energetic enough (about 27 eV) to ionise most atoms.
∴ 4·42 × 10⁻¹⁸.
